These exact House amounts are not Senate training minima or facility ceilings; training is broader than CBP personnel alone. No actual personnel, bonus, vehicle, training or expenditure is inferred. House 60003 adds fiscal year 2025 CBP funds available until September 30, 2029: $1,076,317,000 for named non-intrusive inspection/civil works/AI/machine-learning and other mission support to combat narcotics entry along the named southwest, northern and maritime borders; $2.766 billion for surveillance-technology upgrades/procurement; $673 million for expenses/technology relating to the referenced biometric entry/exit system; $1.234 billion for Air and Marine platforms; and $16 million for screening/vetting/criminal-history databases. Separate DHS purposes receive $500 million for border-security/trafficking efforts and $1 million for border-security commemorations on the same dates. No combined unrestricted account or observed drug/immigration outcome is asserted. The surveillance-tower restriction applies only to subsection (a)(2) funds: the same tower must have both been tested and been accepted by the Federal Government to deliver autonomous capabilities before procurement or deployment with those funds. House defines autonomous as integrated sensor/onboard-computing/AI software and hardware identifying items of interest otherwise identified manually. It is a statutory definition and procurement condition, not a finding about any actual tower or a guarantee of detection accuracy. The House fund/accepting-authority/geographic scope is not replaced by the Senate rule. The complete material pre-vote biometric-system authority preserves the categories already required to provide biometric entry data as the exit-data collection boundary, original program/history and its own integration/training/data-accuracy/access/misuse/correction/appeals conditions. New spending on that referenced system is not first-ever biometric authority, a new every-traveller collection rule, actual processing/data accuracy or a removal/admissibility determination. Existing data protections are source-bound, without guaranteeing any individual correction or asserting operational compliance. Other agency/enforcement and package components remain unfinished. Selected House EOIR and State-incarceration appropriations remain distinct from ICE operations and fees. House 70100 adds $1.25 billion to EOIR for fiscal year 2025, available until September 30, 2029, only to hire necessary support staff and immigration judges and expand courtroom capacity/infrastructure. It does not print the selected Senate November 2028 judge cap; hiring funding does not prove actual hires, courtroom expansion, faster decisions or reduced backlog. House 70111 separately adds $950 million to DOJ for fiscal year 2025, available until September 30, 2029, only for the specified State/political-subdivision incarceration compensation, with the full conviction/status predicates and funding limitation. This is neither all alien incarceration nor an unrestricted payment to every State. The new incarceration-compensation criteria require a felony conviction or at least two misdemeanor convictions in every listed case. In addition, one of three alternatives must hold. The alien entered without inspection or at a time or place not designated by DHS. Alternatively, the alien was subject to removal proceedings when taken into State/local custody. Alternatively, the alien was admitted as a nonimmigrant and, at that custody time, failed to maintain the admitted or changed nonimmigrant status or comply with its conditions. Those entry/proceeding/status alternatives do not remove the common conviction requirement; a charge, one misdemeanor, any noncitizen status or mere encounter is not substituted. They do not themselves establish a new crime, removal ground or individual custody/status/conviction finding. The compensation limitation excludes the State/local entity if it prohibits or in any way restricts the specified federal/State/local personnel from any of the listed activities: immigration-law compliance; federal-enforcement assistance/cooperation; or the named citizenship/status/admissibility/deportability/custody-information inquiries, federal encounter notifications or responses to federal information requests. The incorporated immigration-laws definition includes its named laws, conventions and treaties; it is not new independent State removal authority. This is the printed funding limitation, not a finding that any State is disqualified, a label for every local policy or a conclusion about constitutional enforceability. Complete pre-vote INA 241(i) already provides its own State-incarceration route after a chief-executive written request, with an AG-determined compensation contract or federal-custody alternative, average-cost basis, complete criminal/status definition, priority/security provisions and dated authorization/correctional-purpose limits. Its original exclusion/deportation and Attorney General wording is preserved, distinct from the new removal/DHS wording. No first-ever compensation authority, actual contract/award or current appropriation is inferred. Those old-route fields are not silently imported as new conditions of the self-contained House or Senate funding paragraphs. No actual State compensation, criminal act, judicial decision or observed enforcement outcome is established by these proposed appropriations. Remaining DOJ, reimbursement/removal and other package components remain unfinished. Selected House DOJ drug and prosecution funding remains two distinct appropriations. House 70121 adds $500 million for fiscal year 2025, available until September 30, 2029, only for efforts against drug trafficking, including fentanyl and precursor chemicals, and illegal drug use. That generic drug purpose is not by itself an immigration finding. House 70122 separately adds $600 million on those fiscal/availability dates only to investigate and prosecute its listed immigration matters, gang-related crimes involving aliens, child trafficking and smuggling involving aliens, voting by aliens, Alien Registration Act violations, and violations of or fraud relating to PRWORA title IV, including through DOJ personnel hiring for those matters. The exact House voting phrase is voting by aliens; the Senate phrase is unlawful voting by aliens. This is purpose funding, not a new blanket crime, benefit-eligibility change, finding about every alien or claim that a named person committed a crime. The complete pre-vote 18 U.S.C. 611 voting rule retains its named federal-office scope. Its mixed-election exception requires all three conditions: the election is partly for another purpose; State constitutional/statutory or local-ordinance authority permits alien voting for that other purpose; and that voting is conducted independently so the alien can vote for the other purpose but has no opportunity to vote for the named federal offices. Its separate nonapplication rule also requires all three conditions: each natural parent, or each adoptive parent for an adopted alien, is or was a citizen; permanent U.S. residence before age 16; and reasonable belief in U.S. citizenship at the time of voting. No actual exception, citizenship, voting legality, violation or guilt is determined. These selected funding provisions do not rewrite those exceptions or make every act of alien voting criminal. House does not print the selected Senate 100055 fund, $3.5 billion ceiling, September 2028 availability or January 20 reimbursement rule in these two appropriations. Existing separate House State-border-cost rules are not replaced. No actual investigation, prosecution, hire, drug outcome or expenditure is inferred. Other DOJ/removal and package components remain unfinished. Selected House removal-purpose funding is two distinct additional DHS fiscal year 2025 appropriations available until September 30, 2029. House 70123 provides $75 million only to apply 235(b)(1) to any alien inadmissible under 212(a)(2) or (3), regardless of the period physically present in the United States. House 70124 provides $25 million only to apply 235(c) to an arriving alien whom an immigration officer or immigration judge suspects may be inadmissible under either of those two paragraphs. Actual inadmissibility in the former differs from printed suspicion in the latter; the latter retains the arriving-alien condition. The headings do not establish that every person in either category has been convicted. Neither funding paragraph prints a strike-and-insert amendment of those incorporated procedures. Complete material pre-vote procedural boundaries remain bound, rather than treating these funding titles as findings of conviction or automatic removal. The captured 235(b)(1) screening rule ordinarily names arriving or designated aliens, its subparagraph (F) exception, and officer-determined 212(a)(6)(C) or (7) inadmissibility. The designated-other-alien path requires no admission or parole and failure affirmatively to show continuous physical presence for the immediately preceding two years, under the named discretionary designation authority. An asylum intention or fear of persecution triggers asylum-officer referral/interview under its own conditions. A credible-fear finding leads to detention for further asylum consideration, not an asylum grant. A negative finding retains a written record/notes and requested prompt immigration-judge review, an opportunity to be heard/questioned, the stated practicable-24-hour and hard-seven-day limits, and its own pending/final detention rules. Own pre-interview/review consultation is at no government expense and may not unreasonably delay proceedings. The defined credible-fear standard, officer training/supervision, protected-status review, administrative/collateral-review limits and complete exceptions remain, without a universal no-hearing/no-review claim or guaranteed eligibility. Captured 235(c) ordinarily names arriving-alien suspicion under 212(a)(3)(A), excluding clause (ii), or (B) or (C). Its initial officer/judge order remains subject to AG review, report and no further inquiry/hearing until directed. The AG shall review the order. The AG may order removal without further immigration-judge inquiry/hearing only if satisfied on confidential information of inadmissibility under those named grounds and, after consulting appropriate security agencies, concluding disclosure would prejudice public interest, safety or security. Both conditions are required. If that order is not made, the AG shall specify further inquiry/hearing; the alien or representative may submit a written statement and information. Suspicion is not a conviction or established inadmissibility. Complete 212(a) criminal/security grounds retain their own convictions, admissions, knowledge/reason-to-believe and other standards, exceptions and waiver references. They are not identical to felony conviction or unlawful presence. Full 212(h) and (d)(3) retain named-ground limits, complete alternatives and common conditions, excluded cases and discretionary authorities; no universal waiver or actual individual grant is inferred. Full 242(e) retains limited habeas questions and protected-status proof, District-of-Columbia system challenges with own first-implementation/appeal deadlines, remedy and inquiry limits, not ordinary inadmissibility merits review or an all-court ban. Exact January 29, 2025 Public Law 119-1 is bound with the captured 2024 provisions: its 235(b)(3) State-enforcement route and 242(f)(3) injunction exception retain their own allegations/harm/actor/scope requirements, distinct from individual review. Original 2024 bytes are not relabeled as a complete unamended 2025 Code section. No actual hearing, review, custody, waiver, crime, status or removal outcome is determined. Question 47 reserves precise application of the 70123 funding-purpose grounds/physical-presence wording alongside 235(b)(1) screening/designation/exception/asylum/review boundaries. Question 48 separately reserves 70124 application of broad 212(a)(2)/(3) suspicion alongside 235(c) narrower named grounds and AG review/confidential-information/consultation/written-submission conditions. Exact funding wording and complete inherited procedures remain; no silent repeal, automatic broadened removal, universal loss of asylum/review or individual classifier is accepted. Support/opposition applies only to passage of the entire House proposal; neither component preferences, enactment, legal enforceability nor policy outcomes follow from the vote. Selected exact House floor State Homeland Security Grant Program and Stonegarden funding follow. House floor 60005 common appropriation: In addition to amounts otherwise available, there is appropriated to the Administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency, for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury, not otherwise appropriated, to be administered under the State Homeland Security Grant Program authorized under section 2004 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 605), to enhance State, local, and Tribal security through grants, contracts, cooperative agreements, and other activities, of which-- House floor 60005 purpose 1: $500,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2029, for State and local capabilities to detect, identify, track, or monitor threats from unmanned aircraft systems (as such term is defined in section 44801 of title 49, United States Code); House floor 60005 purpose 2: $625,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2029, for security, planning, and other costs related to the 2026 FIFA World Cup; House floor 60005 purpose 3: $1,000,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2029, for security, planning, and other costs related to the 2028 Olympic Games and 2028 Paralympic Games; and House floor 60005 purpose 4: $450,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2029, for the Operation Stonegarden Grant Program. The pre-vote fiscal year 2024 DHS/FEMA HSGP notice reproduced on Hawaii's official host describes Operation Stonegarden as supporting enhanced cooperation and coordination among CBP, USBP, and Federal, State, local, Tribal and territorial law enforcement agencies to improve overall border security. It funds joint border-security efforts along routes of ingress and egress to and from international borders, including travel corridors in States bordering Mexico and Canada and States and territories with international water borders. In that notice, those State, local, Tribal and territorial law enforcement agencies use their inherent law enforcement authorities and receive no additional authority from participating in Stonegarden. This is dated program-purpose context, not a new power conferred by the House appropriation or a complete 2025 eligibility rule. The floor clause appropriates to the FEMA Administrator additional fiscal year 2025 funds administered under the State Homeland Security Grant Program in 6 U.S.C. 605 for State/local/Tribal security through the printed grant, contract, cooperative-agreement and other activity paths. Each of its four purpose amounts has its own availability until September 30, 2029. The Stonegarden amount is $450,000,000. House FIFA purpose (2) expressly includes planning; House purpose (3) expressly names the 2028 Olympic Games and 2028 Paralympic Games. The Senate prints different event wording; no decision about either version's actual event-expense eligibility is inferred. The House selected text prints no Senate 90005(a)(2) FIFA/Olympics exemption or added consistent-with-titles-18-and-49 phrase. That absence is a source-version comparison, not authority to disregard otherwise applicable law. Generic drone and event funding remain adjacent context without an inferred Immigration purpose. Complete captured 603, 605 and 609 and the dated program notice are reused without changing earlier Senate meanings or declaring their every condition automatically applicable to a House-version grant. House-specific application question 53 remains separate from Senate question 52. No particular grant, entitlement, expenditure, law-enforcement power or individual status result is inferred. Selected exact House 110019 death/disability loan-discharge income-exclusion and SSN provisions follow. House 110019 exclusion grounds: In the case of an individual, gross income does not include any amount which (but for this subsection) would be includible in gross income for such taxable year by reason of the discharge (in whole or in part) of any loan described in subparagraph (B), if such discharge was-- (i) pursuant to subsection (a) or (d) of section 437 of the Higher Education Act of 1965 or the parallel benefit under part D of title IV of such Act (relating to the repayment of loan liability), (ii) pursuant to section 464(c)(1)(F) of such Act, or (iii) otherwise discharged on account of death or total and permanent disability of the student. House 110019 loan categories: A loan is described in this subparagraph if such loan is-- (i) a student loan (as defined in paragraph (2)), or (ii) a private education loan (as defined in section 140(a) of the Consumer Credit Protection Act (15 U.S.C. 1650(a)). House 110019 identification and own marital rules: (i) In general.--Subparagraph (A) shall not apply with respect to any discharge during any taxable year unless the taxpayer includes on the return of tax for such taxable year-- (I) the taxpayer's social security number, and (II) if the taxpayer is married, the social security number of such taxpayers's spouse. (ii) Social security number.--For purposes of this subparagraph, the term `social security number' has the meaning given such term in section 24(h)(7). (iii) Married individuals.--Rules similar to the rules of section 32(d) shall apply to this subparagraph.. House 110019 math-error amendment: Section 6213(g)(2) is amended by striking and at the end of subparagraph (U), by striking the period at the end of subparagraph (V) and inserting , and, and by inserting after subparagraph (V) the following new subparagraph: (W) an omission of a correct social security number required under section 108(f)(5)(C) (relating to discharges on account of death or disability).. House 110019 discharge-date applicability: The amendments made by this section shall apply to discharges after December 31, 2025. The common requirement that the discharged loan meet new subparagraph (B) applies across all three ground alternatives. Original (f)(1) service-conditioned discharge and (4) named repayment-program exclusions remain separate. This does not mean every education-related debt qualifies. The three exclusion-ground alternatives remain separate: the first two use their specified HEA discharge paths, while only the third prints otherwise discharged on account of death or total and permanent disability of the student. A parent borrower is not silently equated to the student. Full 437(a) retains qualifying loans, death/disability determinations, safeguards, conditional reinstatement, VA documentation and own income-monitoring/approval/opt-out/update rules; 437(d) separately addresses a parent loan when the student dies. Captured 464(c)(1)(F) retains loan-fund agreement scope, borrower death, regulated permanent/total disability, the medically determinable substantial-gainful-activity alternative with its own duration/death tests, and VA unemployability due to service-connected disability. Part D parallel benefit is retained with complete captured 455 and its unless-otherwise-specified limitation, not a universal cancellation promise. Selected exact House account and separate pilot eligibility clauses follow. House 110115 account establishment and instrument: The term `TRUMP account' means a trust created or organized in the United States for the exclusive benefit of an individual and which is designated (in such manner as the Secretary shall prescribe) at the time of the establishment of the trust as a TRUMP account, but only if the written governing instrument creating the trust meets the following requirements: (A) The individual establishing the account shall provide to the trustee the social security number of such individual and of the account beneficiary. (B) Except in the case of a qualified rollover contribution described in subsection (e), no contribution will be accepted-- (i) before January 1, 2026, (ii) unless it is in cash, (iii) unless the account beneficiary has not attained age 18, and (iv) if such contribution would result in aggregate contributions for the taxable year exceeding the contribution limit specified in subsection (c)(1). (C) No distribution (other than a distribution of a qualified rollover contribution) will be allowed-- (i) before the date on which the account beneficiary attains age 18, or (ii) in the case of such an account the account beneficiary of which has not attained age 25, if the aggregate distributions from such account exceeds the amount that is \1/2\ the cash equivalent value of the account on the date on which the account beneficiary attains age 18. (D) The account beneficiary has not attained age 8 on the date of the establishment of the account. (E) The trustee is a bank (as defined in section 408(n)) or another person who demonstrates to the satisfaction of the Secretary that the manner in which that person will administer the trust will be consistent with the requirements of this section or who has so demonstrated with respect to any individual retirement plan. (F) The interest of an individual in the balance of his account is nonforfeitable. (G) The assets of the trust shall not be commingled with other property except in a common trust fund or common investment fund. (H) No part of the trust funds will be invested in any asset other than eligible investments. House 110115 account beneficiary: The term `account beneficiary' means the individual on whose behalf the TRUMP account was established. House 110115 tax-year applicability: The amendments made by this section shall apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. House 110116 one-time credit and account-only payment: In the case of any taxpayer with respect to whom an eligible individual is a qualifying child, there shall be allowed a one-time credit of $1,000 with respect to each such eligible individual who is a qualifying child of such taxpayer which shall be payable by the Secretary only to the TRUMP account with respect to which such eligible individual is the account beneficiary. House 110116 Secretary account establishment and opt-out: (1) In general.--In the case of any eligible individual that the Secretary determines is not the account beneficiary of any TRUMP account as of the qualifying date of such eligible individual, the Secretary shall establish an account for the benefit of such eligible individual. (2) Qualifying date.--For purposes of paragraph (1), the term `qualifying date' means, with respect to an eligible individual, the first date on which a return of tax is filed by an individual with respect to whom such eligible individual is a qualifying child with respect to the taxable year to which such return relates. (3) Notification.--In the case of any eligible individual for the benefit of whom the Secretary establishes an account under paragraph (1), the Secretary shall-- (A) notify any individual with respect to whom such eligible individual is a qualifying child for the taxable year described in paragraph (2) of the establishment of such account, and (B) shall provide an opportunity to such individual to elect to decline the application of this subsection to such qualifying child. (4) Determination of default trustee.--For purposes of selecting a trustee for an account established under paragraph (1), the Secretary shall take into account-- (A) the history of reliability and regulatory compliance of such trustee, (B) the customer service experience of such trustee, (C) the costs imposed by such trustee on the account or account beneficiary, and (D) to the extent practicable, the preferences of any individual described in paragraph (3)(A) with respect to such eligible individual. House 110116 pilot birth window and citizenship at birth: For purposes of subsection (a), the term eligible individual means an individual-- (1) who is born after December 31, 2024, and before January 1, 2029, and (2) who is a United States citizen at birth. House 110116 pilot return identification: (1) In general.--No credit shall be allowed under subsection (a) to a taxpayer unless such taxpayer includes on the return of tax for the taxable year-- (A) such individual's social security number, (B) if such individual is married, the social security number of such individual's spouse, and (C) the social security number of the eligible individual with respect to whom such credit is allowed. (2) Social security number defined.--For purposes of paragraph (1), the term `social security number' shall have the meaning given such term in section 24(h)(7). House 110116 pilot definitions: For purposes of this section-- (1) Qualifying child.--The term qualifying child has the meaning given such term in section 152(c). (2) TRUMP account; account beneficiary.--The terms `TRUMP account' and `account beneficiary' have the meaning given such terms in section 530A(b).. House 110116 improper-claim penalty and incorporated definitions: In the case of any taxpayer that makes an excessive claim for a credit under section 6434-- (1) if such excess is a result of negligence or disregard of the rules or regulations, there shall be imposed a penalty of $500, or (2) if such excess is a result of fraud, there shall be imposed a penalty of $1,000. (b) Definitions.--The terms `negligence' and `disregard' have the same meaning as when such terms are used in section 6662.. House 110116 math-error amendment: Section 6213(g)(2), as amended by the preceding provisions of this Act, is amended by striking and at the end of subparagraph (Y), by striking the period at the end of subparagraph (Z) and inserting , and, and by inserting after subparagraph (Z) the following new subparagraph: (AA) an omission of a correct social security number required under section 6434(d)(1) (relating to the TRUMP accounts contribution pilot program).. House 110116 tax-year applicability: The amendments made by this section shall apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Selected exact House tips and overtime deduction/identification clauses follow. House 110101 deduction and reporting gate: There shall be allowed as a deduction an amount equal to the qualified tips received during the taxable year that are included on statements furnished to the individual pursuant to section 6041(d)(3), 6041A(e)(3), 6050W(f)(2), 6051(a)(18), or reported by the taxpayer on Form 4137 (or successor). House 110101 business receipt/expense limit: In the case of qualified tips received by an individual during any taxable year in the course of any trade or business of such individual, such qualified tips shall be taken into account under subsection (a) only to the extent that the gross receipts of the taxpayer from such trade or business for such taxable year (including such qualified tips) exceeds the sum of-- (1) cost of goods sold that are allocable to such receipts, plus (2) other expenses, losses, or deductions (other than the deduction allowed under this section), which are properly allocable to such receipts. House 110101 qualified-tip conditions: For purposes of this section-- (1) In general.--The term `qualified tip' means any cash tip received by an individual in an occupation which traditionally and customarily received tips on or before December 31, 2024, as provided by the Secretary. (2) Exclusions.--Such term shall not include any amount received by an individual unless-- (A) such amount is paid voluntarily without any consequence in the event of nonpayment, is not the subject of negotiation, and is determined by the payor, (B) the trade or business in the course of which the individual receives such amount is not a specified service trade or business (as defined in section 199A(d)(2)), (C) such individual does not receive earned income (within the meaning of section 32) in excess of the dollar amount in effect under section 414(q)(1)(B)(i) for the calendar year in which the taxable year begins, and (D) such other requirements as may be established by the Secretary in regulations or other guidance are satisfied. House 110101 identification and own marital rules: (1) In general.--No deduction shall be allowed under this section unless the taxpayer includes on the return of tax for the taxable year-- (A) such individual's social security number, and (B) if the individual is married, the social security number of such individual's spouse. (2) Married individuals.--Rules similar to the rules of section 32(d) shall apply to this section. (3) Social security number defined.--For purposes of paragraph (1), the term `social security number' shall have the meaning given such term in section 24(h)(7).. House 110101 anti-reclassification regulations: The Secretary shall prescribe such regulations or other guidance as may be necessary to prevent reclassification of income as qualified tips, including regulations or other guidance to prevent abuse of the deduction allowed by this section. House 110101 deduction termination: No deduction shall be allowed under this section for any taxable year beginning after December 31, 2028.. This July3 House concurrence concerns the Senate's July1 EAS, which strikes all after the first word and replaces the earlier H.R.1 text. It is the complete multi-domain reconciliation replacement, not a second passage of the unchanged House bill or a separate vote on its Immigration components. Selected Immigration highlights here concern border infrastructure, detention and asylum fees; other immigration-related benefits, taxes, employment authorization, child-sponsor, reimbursement and enforcement provisions are not exhaustively described. Section90001 would appropriate an additional $46.55billion for fiscal2025 to CBP, available until September30,2029, for new/replacement primary, waterborne and secondary barriers, access roads, detection attributes and ground preparation for CBP operations and barrier construction/maintenance. The different House60001 accounts are not silently used to define this replacement amount or its purposes. Section90003 would appropriate an additional $45billion for fiscal2025 to ICE, available until September30,2029, for single-adult alien detention and family residential-center capacity. Aliens MAY be detained at family centers pending an INA removal decision and, if ordered removed, until removal. Single-adult detention standards are set in the Secretary's discretion CONSISTENT WITH APPLICABLE LAW. The family-center definition covers apprehended/encountered family units, including children who are not statutorily defined unaccompanied alien children, and does not reproduce the House's express regardless-of-State-licensing clause.6USC279(g)(2) requires no lawful immigration status, under18 age, and no US parent/legal guardian or none available for care/physical custody. Neither the capacity funding nor permission establishes automatic detention/removal of every alien, elimination of all legal constraints or actual operations. Section100002 requires an additional fee upon filing an asylum application. The fiscal2025 amount is the greater of $100 or the amount set by DHS/the Attorney General, as applicable, by rule; it cannot be waived/reduced. From fiscal2026 the prior fiscal-year fee is increased by the printed July-to-July CPI-U increment rounded down to a multiple of $10. Half of Attorney-General-filed receipts go to EOIR; half of DHS-filed receipts go to USCIS's existing Immigration Examinations Fee Account, retained/expended without further appropriation; uncredited receipts go to Treasury. This $100 filing floor differs from the House's $1,000 floor. Section100009 separately requires an additional fee for EACH CALENDAR YEAR an asylum application remains pending. Its fiscal2025 amount is the greater of $100 or a DHS rule amount, followed by the printed CPI-U annual adjustment with the increment rounded DOWN TO THE NEAREST DOLLAR; receipts go to Treasury and the fee cannot be waived/reduced. Do not transfer that rounding to the initial-filing fee or back to the House's differently printed yearly formula. The termination date is not measured from receipt or sending of the notice; the review deadline is not the termination date. No identical grace period is promised to every later applicant, perpetual grandfathering, actual completed review, actual termination or observed administrative outcome is inferred. Enactment-relative dates are not converted into dates based on this vote or the later enacted law. Senate category(3) instead requires an alien who HAS BEEN GRANTED Cuban and Haitian entrant status as defined in 501(e). The complete definition retains the special-parole/subsequent-special-status category's service-time wording, and the OTHER Cuban/Haitian-national category's (parole with NO other-acquired-INA-status OR removal proceedings OR pending asylum) AND NO final/nonappealable/legally-enforceable removal-order grouping. The no-order modifier stays in the latter category and the no-other-status modifier in its parole alternative; nationality or service-time wording does not prove an actual grant. House 203(a)-petition/visa/program predicates are not imported. The restriction applies to the existing-enrollee cohort EIGHTEEN MONTHS AFTER ENACTMENT, with review completed NOT LATER THAN ONE YEAR AFTER ENACTMENT and each identified person's comprehensible notice tied to that eighteen-month termination date. This is not an eighteen-month period from notice or a guarantee of six months between notice and termination. Senate sections 71301/71302 propose their own ACA status and special-income-rule changes. The selected ACA status provision adds lawfully present aliens who are NOT eligible aliens to 36B(e)(1), whose named condition concerns one or more individuals for whom the taxpayer is allowed a section 151 deduction (including taxpayer or spouse), and whose complete existing mechanism reduces the portion of counted premiums attributable to the affected INDIVIDUAL and adjusts family-size/household-income calculations using the specified fraction or comparable method. It is not automatic loss of every otherwise eligible household member's credit or a blanket ban on insurance enrollment. Existing 36B(e)(2) whole-period citizenship/nationality/lawful-presence wording is retained as subparagraph(A); the new eligible-alien provision concerns an individual who IS AN ALIEN AND LAWFULLY PRESENT and who IS, AND IS REASONABLY EXPECTED TO BE FOR THE ENTIRE CREDIT-ENROLLMENT PERIOD, within its own listed LPR, version-specific Cuban-related, OR COFA-lawful-residence category. Both current status and the reasonable whole-period expectation remain, common to the listed alternatives; a single day of status, nationality alone or any lawful temporary stay is not substituted. Citizens/US nationals are not required to fit the new alien-only list. Separate applicable-taxpayer, income, coverage-month, plan/enrollment and other credit requirements remain; status alone is not sufficient. The companion provision deletes 36B(c)(1)(B), whose complete pre-vote special rule requires ALL of household income NOT GREATER THAN 100 percent of the family poverty line, LAWFUL PRESENCE as an alien, AND Medicaid ineligibility BY REASON OF THAT ALIEN STATUS, then treats that taxpayer as applicable with income equal to 100 percent for credit purposes. It is not every Medicaid-ineligible person, any low income or a finding that the person lacks lawful presence. Deletion removes that special treatment for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025; it does not alone prove that EVERY person at EXACTLY 100 percent loses the credit, because ordinary (c)(1)(A) begins at 100 percent subject to its other rules. The temporary 2021-2025 upper-income rule and complete coverage predicates are separately bound, without extending it into future years or quantifying an actual credit. The status provision's non-conforming amendments apply to TAXABLE YEARS BEGINNING AFTER DECEMBER 31, 2026; its conforming amendments apply to PLAN YEARS BEGINNING ON OR AFTER JANUARY 1, 2027. Those tax/plan-year bases remain distinct from the earlier special-rule repeal; neither vote date nor later enacted implementation dates are substituted. Both status versions replace the lawful-alien phrase in 5000A(d)(3) with the eligible-alien reference; they do NOT change the bound penalty calculation's existing zero-dollar/zero-percent components. No revived monetary mandate penalty or actual tax/benefit determination is inferred. Senate 36B(e)(2)(B) prints IF, preserving that wording rather than substituting the House IF AND ONLY IF. Its category(ii) requires HAS BEEN GRANTED defined Cuban/Haitian entrant status, subject to the same current status AND reasonable expectation for the entire credit-enrollment period. Complete 501(e) keeps special parole/subsequent special status distinct from OTHER Cuban/Haitian nationals whose own (parole-with-no-other-status OR removal-proceedings OR pending-asylum) alternatives share NO final/nonappealable/legally-enforceable removal order. Modifiers remain in their own branch; nationality/service-time wording does not establish a grant. No House family-petition/visa/parole-program conjunction is imported. Senate 71301 adds eligible-alien verification/attestation to the named 1411 provisions, but its (c)(1)(C) attestation extension concerns premium tax credits alone, where House text also names reduced cost-sharing. Its 1412(d) insertion concerns CREDITS UNDER 36B for aliens not eligible, where House text inserts a broader individual disqualifier into the federal-payments provision. It has no direct counterpart to the selected House 1402(e)/1331(e)(1) status amendments. Senate 71302 deletes 36B(c)(1)(B) without the House renumbering, basic-health branch removal or cost-sharing sentence deletion. The remaining pre-vote 1402(b) text references the removed 36B(c)(1)(B); application to residual cost-sharing/basic-health rules is separately reserved. Absence of direct Senate amendments does not prove continuing awards, automatic loss or resolved effects of those cross-references. General Exchange verification provisions are a separate description and do not become an insurance-enrollment ban through this credit-status summary. Senate section 71303 proposes its own Exchange premium-credit verification and filing-compliance conditions. The selected Exchange verification provision adds credit coverage-month conditions for an INDIVIDUAL enrolled in a qualified health plan through an Exchange. A month beginning BEFORE the specified verification is excluded unless the own past-month verification clause is met; this is not an assertion that all earlier months are permanently lost. Applicable information must be PROVIDED OR VERIFIED BY THE APPLICANT, with affirmation of at least the listed information TO THE EXTENT RELEVANT to the specified eligibility. Both versions expressly say failure of this paragraph ALONE does NOT make an individual ineligible to enroll through the Exchange for that month. Credit coverage-month, advance payment, reduced cost-sharing and enrollment are distinct; no insurance-enrollment ban, actual credit award/loss or guaranteed verification date is inferred. Both versions separately exclude a plan from the tax provision's qualified-health-plan definition UNLESS the Exchange PROVIDES a pre-enrollment verification PROCESS through which ANY APPLICANT MAY, BEGINNING NOT LATER THAN AUGUST 1, verify the version-specific information/eligibility for plans in the SUBSEQUENT PLAN YEAR. This is an Exchange process availability deadline, not a requirement that each applicant must submit or complete verification by August 1, a universal enrollment period or a promise of coverage. Amendments in these selected sections apply to TAXABLE YEARS BEGINNING AFTER DECEMBER 31, 2027; the incorporated Senate rule's post-2025 scope is not substituted as the statute's effective date. Senate coverage-month verification requires enrollment eligibility AND eligibility for ANY advance premium credit payment; it has NO House reduced-cost-sharing third prong. Its information list pairs HOUSEHOLD INCOME AND FAMILY SIZE and asks WHETHER THE INDIVIDUAL IS AN ELIGIBLE ALIEN, alongside coverage, residence and authorized other necessary information. Past-month verification prints IF, without importing the House IF AND ONLY IF, and retains own enrollment/advance-credit eligibility FOR THAT MONTH. The Secretary MAY waive ONLY subparagraph (A) for an individual enrolling for ONE OR MORE taxable-year months DURING an Exchange special enrollment period BASED ON CHANGE IN THAT INDIVIDUAL'S FAMILY SIZE; it is not an automatic waiver, every special enrollment period or a waiver of all other credit requirements. Exchanges may use ANY AVAILABLE DATA AND RELIABLE third-party sources in collecting information FOR VERIFICATION BY THE APPLICANT; permission does not make every third-party source reliable or eliminate applicant verification. The Senate filing-compliance clause names ONLY 45 CFR 155.305(f)(4)(iii) AS PUBLISHED JUNE 25, 2025 (90 FR 27074), APPLIED AS THOUGH TO ALL PLAN YEARS AFTER 2025. The final rule's printed (iii) says PLAN YEAR 2026 ONLY and supplies the one-year filing/reconciliation condition and its own tax-information-protecting notice alternatives; the bill expressly changes that referenced duration. The rule's separate introductory two-consecutive-year baseline is not substituted for the named (iii), nor is the House March proposal. The condition retains HHS notification, prior advances for filer OR married-couple spouse, the year whose tax data would be used, and failure to file/reconcile for that period. Direct failure notification to the filer OR indirect risk/education notification to filer/enrollee remains; there is no guarantee of a fixed notice-to-loss interval. The Senate pre-enrollment process covers verification of the applicant's HOUSEHOLD INCOME AND ELIGIBILITY FOR ENROLLMENT for the subsequent plan year, without importing the House advance-credit/cost-sharing list. This section has no direct counterpart to the selected House 44201(b)(1) statutory missing-data/discrepancy additions. Absence of that direct amendment does not establish that no other verification rules apply or that the House exception determines Senate awards. Residual program/application questions remain separately reserved. The Senate ACA candidate now binds the complete pre-vote cost-sharing credit dependency identified by independent source-completeness review. Complete pre-vote section 1402(g) adds a material boundary to the selected ACA cost-sharing comparison: NO cost-sharing reduction is allowed for coverage for ANY MONTH UNLESS that month is a COVERAGE MONTH FOR WHICH A SECTION 36B CREDIT IS ALLOWED TO THE INSURED OR AN APPLICABLE TAXPAYER ON THE INSURED'S BEHALF. This is a necessary credit/month dependency, not a sufficient entitlement, and it does not require every insured to be the tax filer personally. Shared terms take section 36B meanings; eligibility data use the taxable year of the ADVANCE DETERMINATION, not the taxable year for which the credit is allowed. Retaining a cost-sharing sentence or basic-health branch alone therefore does not establish continuing reductions or an award. Individual/family calculations, own program predicates and the direct House/Senate amendment distinctions remain; residual cross-reference/program application stays RESERVED as question 34. No individual credit, reduction or basic-health outcome is adjudicated. Senate section 70604 proposes a 1 PERCENT remittance tax under its own physical-funding and noncash provisions. Both selected remittance sections require the SENDER to pay the tax, the PROVIDER to collect it FROM THE SENDER AND remit QUARTERLY as prescribed by the Secretary, and secondary provider liability ONLY TO THE EXTENT the tax is unpaid at transfer AND not collected. These are separate payer, collection and secondary-liability roles, not a tax only on providers or a charge already observed. Both deem the remittance a financing transaction for the specified multiple-party anti-conduit authority; existing 7701(l) permits appropriate regulation/recharacterization, not an automatic finding of evasion or wrongdoing. Transfer amendments apply to TRANSFERS MADE AFTER DECEMBER 31, 2025, not the vote date or a substituted later enacted date. The bound remittance definitions concern an ELECTRONIC, PROVIDER-INITIATED funds transfer requested by a CONSUMER/NATURAL-PERSON SENDER LOCATED IN A DEFINED STATE to an AUTHORIZED DESIGNATED RECIPIENT LOCATED IN A FOREIGN COUNTRY. Consumer/State, electronic and normal-course provider definitions are independently bound, with account-independence and the statutory SMALL-VALUE EXCLUSION retained. This is not every domestic payment, every cross-border business transaction, every family expense or a recipient-citizenship test. Electronic transfer technology and the Senate physical FUNDING instrument are different predicates. No specific transaction, person, provider, regulatory threshold or actual tax outcome is classified. The Senate tax applies ONLY where the sender provides CASH, MONEY ORDER, CASHIER'S CHECK OR ANOTHER SIMILAR PHYSICAL INSTRUMENT AS THE SECRETARY DETERMINES to the provider, and remains subject to its SEPARATE NONAPPLICATION provisions. Nonapplication covers funds WITHDRAWN FROM AN ACCOUNT held in/by an institution BOTH DESCRIBED IN 31 USC 5312(a)(2)(A)-(H) AND SUBJECT TO SUBCHAPTER II OF CHAPTER 53 requirements, OR funds PROVIDED WITH A DEBIT OR CREDIT CARD ISSUED IN THE US. The listed-institution AND regulatory-subjection conditions are conjunctive; not every institution or any card regardless of issuance suffices. Cash-only language is not used to erase a separately applicable nonapplication or classify intermediate withdrawals/funding paths. Complete debit/card definitions retain network/asset-account and no-paper-check scope; the bill says WITHOUT REGARD TO debit-definition (B), rather than an automatic exclusion of every possible prepaid card. The inherited credit-device definition is separately bound, with the US-issuance condition additional. The Senate prints EFTA 919(g) for remittance and 920(c)(2)/(3) for card definitions, matching the bound source-credit crosswalk; it has no counterpart to the selected House verified citizen/national-provider exception, new 36C credit or 6050BB reporting scheme. Those missing counterparts do not establish a citizenship-based Senate tax exemption or a person's final cost. All own funding/exclusion and statutory-definition predicates must be retained; no universal 1% charge on all remittances or outcome for a particular immigrant is inferred. The selected Senate ACA comparison remains its own 71301/71302/71303 eligible-alien, income-floor and verification mechanisms described above, with their respective tax/plan-year dates. Their complete operative sections do not contain the House 44201(i) named-June-2012-DACA amendments. No House title-wide, cost-sharing-section or preceding-Federal-payment-sentence exclusion is imported into those Senate clauses, and their own eligible-alien restrictions remain. This selected-section comparison does not claim Senate eligibility for every DACA recipient or whole-package absence of every possible DACA effect; the original memo is not a current ACA eligibility decision. Selected Senate section 70104 requires the qualifying child's defined SSN in either case. The taxpayer must also include the taxpayer's defined SSN or, on a joint return, the defined SSN of at least one spouse. This is not both spouses on every joint return, a child SSN alone, or a grant to every mixed-status household. It does not add the House SIMILAR-32(d) clause, so that new House marital rule is not imported. Its amendments apply to TAXABLE YEARS BEGINNING AFTER DECEMBER 31, 2024. Full section context extends 24(h), prints $2,200 rather than the House temporary $2,500/later $2,000 structure, and uses its own after-2025 credit-amount inflation with base-year substitution and rounding. Own refundable ceiling/inflation and the underlying credit conditions remain; no actual indexed amount/refund is calculated. Selected same-bill 70103 zero-exemption extension retains the reference rule, with its own after-2024 date; its separate senior-deduction/SSN mechanism is addressed below. The child-credit comparison is with the complete pre-vote 24(a)-(h), not its separate historical 2021 regime. Before either amendment, 24(h)(7) required the QUALIFYING CHILD'S defined SSN; the new clauses add claimant-side conditions without changing that child prerequisite. An SSN is not alone citizenship proof. Both new definitions permit SSA issuance to either a US citizen or an individual under the named work-authorized-alien branch, including the specified catch-up portion. In either case, the SSN must have been issued before the due date for the return. Any other SSA issuance purpose or an ITIN does not alone satisfy this definition. Complete SSA issuance text distinguishes those branches. Section 24(c) retains an incorporated 152(c) qualifying child AND its own NOT-ATTAINED-17 requirement and its separate citizenship/residence limitation; complete 152 preserves relationship, abode/support, joint-return/refund, competing-claim, adopted/foster, custody/release and missing-child exceptions. Neither a valid SSN nor a citizenship label establishes all credit prerequisites. Own income/phaseout, earned-income/refund, tax/identification/year and other conditions remain; credit/refund figures are not guaranteed payments. Retained 24(h)(4) is separate: (A) provides a $500 other-dependent branch with own (B) noncitizen boundary, and (C) says a qualifying child not allowed credit BY REASON OF PARAGRAPH (7) is treated as a dependent to whom (A) applies. Neither bill strikes that text. Its application to newly added taxpayer/spouse SSN failures is RESERVED as question 39; no automatic fallback award, complete household-credit loss or claim about every dependent is made. Pre-vote 151(d)(5)(B) says reducing the exemption amount to zero is NOT TAKEN INTO ACCOUNT in determining allowed/allowable/entitled deductions for OTHER TITLE PROVISIONS, so zero exemptions alone do not establish no child credit. The exact same-bill 151(d)(5) amendments extend the zero-exemption period while retaining that reference rule; distinct own dates and separately addressed Senate senior provisions are not merged into this child-credit description. Both amend 6213(g)(2)(I) from section 24(e) to SECTION 24 for omission of a correct identification number; this mathematical-or-clerical-error mechanism is not a finding of fraud, corruption, an actual debt or removal of all remedies. Complete 6213(b)(1)/(2) requires notice of the alleged error AND explanation, distinguishes that notice from a deficiency notice/no petition BASED ON THAT NOTICE, permits an abatement request WITHIN 60 DAYS AFTER NOTICE IS SENT, requires abatement UPON RECEIPT of that request, subjects reassessment to deficiency procedures and stays levy/court collection during the abatement period. No actual notice, filing deadline, assessment, successful claim or taxpayer classification is inferred. Senate section 70103 adds its own section 151(d)(5)(C) deduction of $6,000 for each qualified individual in a taxable year beginning before January 1, 2029, subject to its effective date for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. There are two listed person alternatives: the taxpayer, or the taxpayer's spouse on a joint return. In either case, the claimed person must have attained 65 before the tax year closes and that person's defined SSN must be included on the return. One spouse's number alone does not establish deductions for both seniors. The amount is reduced, but not below zero, by 6 percent of modified adjusted gross income over $75,000, or over $150,000 on a joint return. If the taxpayer is married within the meaning of section 7703, this subparagraph applies only if the taxpayer and spouse file a joint return. The new House similar-32(d) provision and hypothetical-itemizer mechanism are not imported. This own deduction accompanies the extended zero-exemption/reference rules rather than replacing every existing aged standard amount or exempting all Social Security income. The inherited SSN definition is the same version's amended section 24(h)(7). It permits SSA issuance to either a US citizen or an individual under the named work-authorized-alien branch, including the specified catch-up portion. In either case, the number must have been issued before the due date for the return. An ITIN or any other SSA number does not alone satisfy the definition, and the listed alien branch is not citizenship-only. The child-credit joint-return alternative does not replace the senior deduction's identification condition. Full marital authorities retain their own reference scopes and conditional separated-spouse rules; this description does not determine anyone's marital status. Complete section 63 preserves taxable-income and itemization mechanics and its own standard-deduction exclusions, including a nonresident alien individual. Section 151 retains its own spouse/exemption references and zero-exemption rule for other-provision deduction references. These are source-bound prerequisites, rather than eligibility for every alien, senior or itemizer or an accepted override of an exclusion. A deduction is not a dollar-for-dollar credit, an exemption of all Social Security benefits or a guaranteed refund. Both versions' senior amendments apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Each version retains its own printed limit for a taxable year beginning before January 1, 2029. Both modified-income definitions add amounts excluded under sections 911, 931 and 933. No personal amount, return, age, marriage, residency or tax outcome is determined. Each adds its own mathematical-error omission reference: House (Z) names its section 63(f)(5)(D), while Senate (W) names its section 151(d)(5)(C). Those labels and provisions are not interchangeable. The inherited notice rules require an alleged error and explanation; the no-petition rule concerns a petition based on that notice. An abatement request may be filed within 60 days after the notice is sent. On receipt of that request the assessment must be abated, any reassessment uses deficiency procedures, and levy/court collection is stayed during the abatement period. No actual debt, fraud or loss of every remedy is inferred. Selected Senate section 70606 requires the individual's defined SSN on the return for both education credits. If the credit concerns qualified tuition and related expenses of an individual other than the taxpayer or spouse, that other individual's name and defined SSN are also required. The individual-number requirement applies in either expense case. It does not add the House conditional spouse-number clause or the House amendment to section 25A(g)(6). The retained married-individual rule applies only if a taxpayer married within section 7703 files a joint return with the spouse. Absence of a new spouse-number clause is not separate-return eligibility, and the child-credit at-least-one-spouse alternative is not an education-credit rule. Both selected education sections replace section 25A(g)(1), whose subsection (a) covers the American Opportunity Tax Credit and Lifetime Learning Credit. Before amendment, the general student name and taxpayer-identification-number rule applied to both credits, while the additional student/taxpayer issuance-date and institution-number rules were AOTC-specific. The new defined-SSN condition applies to both credits. Both inherit their own same-bill amended section 24(h)(7) definition: SSA issuance to either a US citizen or the named work-authorized-alien branch, including its specified catch-up portion. In either case, the number must have been issued before the return due date. Any SSA number or an ITIN does not alone meet that definition; it is not citizenship-only. The old AOTC student deadline says on or before the due date, while the new definition says before. Those exact bounds are preserved. Child-credit claimant alternatives and senior each-person rules do not replace the education section's named roles. Both new institution clauses concern only the American Opportunity Tax Credit: the taxpayer must include the employer identification number of any institution to which the taxpayer paid qualified tuition and related expenses taken into account under section 25A on the tax-year return. That is not a new institution-number requirement for Lifetime Learning or for every institution irrespective of the named payments. Expenses paid by a qualifying dependent retain section 25A(g)(3)'s treatment as paid by the other taxpayer; the dependent cannot independently claim the credit under that paragraph. Full dependent and zero-exemption reference conditions remain, without an individual family determination. Material credit prerequisites remain. AOTC has its per-student, election, four-prior-year, first-four-postsecondary-years, eligible-academic-period, half-time and named felony-drug/prior-claim restrictions. Lifetime Learning has its per-taxpayer expense and job-skills/course context. Own income phaseouts, excluded-income additions, expense definitions and nonacademic/sports exclusions, assistance reductions, prepayments, double-benefit prohibition, payee-statement exception, partial-AOTC-refund/child restriction and recapture authority remain. A defined number is necessary under the new identification clause, rather than proof of all student, expense, credit or refund prerequisites. The AOTC eligible-student reference names HEA 484(a)(1), as in effect when section 25A was enacted, and separately requires at least half the normal full-time course load. It does not name the whole of current 484(a), including its separate citizenship paragraph. The institution definition separately requires the frozen HEA 481 description and eligibility to participate in a title IV program. Code reference notes identify the frozen date as August 5, 1997. Historical 1996 and 1997 witnesses preserve the selected student enrollment/credential provision, its preparatory-course and teacher-credential exceptions, and the complete referenced institution conditions, including their incorporated historical definitions. Selected student and incorporated institution-definition passages match exactly; full HEA 481 operative words match only after two declared split-word comparisons. Original texts remain unchanged. Annual dates alone do not establish personal or institutional eligibility, and neither current student-aid eligibility nor a new House student-aid provision is silently substituted for those frozen tax references. The retained nonresident rule applies if the taxpayer was a nonresident alien for any portion of the tax year. Section 25A applies only if that individual is treated as a resident for chapter 1 by a section 6013(g) or (h) election. The (g) path requires the named nonresident individual at year close to be married to a citizen or resident and both spouses to make the election. Its duration, neither-spouse-resident nonapplication, termination and re-election limits remain. The (h) path requires nonresident status at year beginning, resident status at year close, marriage at year close to a citizen or resident, and both individuals' prescribed election; its own one-election limit remains. Tax-resident treatment for the specified chapters does not grant immigration status, work authorization, citizenship or a credit automatically. This is not a categorical denial to every noncitizen. Both sections apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. Both replace the TIN language in mathematical-error section 6213(g)(2)(J) with social security number or employer identification number. The retained notice rules require an alleged error and explanation; the no-petition rule concerns a petition based on that notice. An abatement request may be filed within 60 days after the notice is sent. Receipt requires abatement; reassessment uses deficiency procedures and collection is stayed during the abatement period. No actual debt, wrongdoing, personal return or loss of every remedy is inferred. Selected Senate 100052(8) uses the $29.85 billion additional fiscal year 2025 ICE appropriation, available through September 30, 2029, for its listed purposes; it does not earmark the entire account or a separate House $20 million for family unity. Its family-unity purpose maintains care and custody during the pending specified charge, expressly in accordance with applicable laws, and detains the alien with the alien's child. Both conditions must hold: the alien is charged only with a misdemeanor under INA 275(a), and entered the United States with the alien's child who has not attained 18 years. The charge is not a conviction or proof of wrongdoing; the complete entry statute distinguishes its own first/subsequent and other provisions. This is the selected accompanied-parent/child funding purpose, not all family detention, the UAC category or actual co-detention. The express applicable-laws wording is preserved for this Senate clause without adding it to the House printed clause or adjudicating either's legal constraints. House 70115-70119 UAC capacity, examinations, disclosure and withdrawal provisions are not substituted for this exact Senate family-unity purpose. Other enforcement/package components remain unfinished. Selected Senate 100052 personnel and operations purposes share the $29.85 billion additional fiscal year 2025 ICE account, available through September 30, 2029. They are not separate House account amounts or individual earmarks of the entire envelope. Paragraph (1) funds hiring and training additional officers, agents, investigators and support staff, prioritizing/streamlining retired ICE hires, without importing the House printed yearly hiring minima. Paragraph (2) permits the Director to give discretionary performance bonuses for exemplary service and retention bonuses for two additional years of enforcement service. Signing bonuses may go to an agent, officer or attorney both hired on or after enactment and committing to five years of that service. Unlike the House signing clause, this is may, not shall. A retention/signing bonus requires the written service-period/amount/payment/early-termination agreement, with its own terms. No bonus, hiring or exemplary-performance outcome is inferred. Paragraph (3) supports recruitment/hiring/onboarding through IT, recruitment/marketing and necessary staff. Paragraph (4) funds transportation and related costs associated with departure or removal operations. Paragraphs (5)-(7) fund enforcement/removal IT including fee collections, facility upgrades and fleet modernization. The Senate fee-collection wording is not replaced by House fine-and-penalty wording; funding does not establish actual fees collected, debts or removal orders. Paragraph (9) funds expanding, facilitating and implementing 287(g) agreements; full material pre-vote qualification/training/law/supervision/written-power/duration/voluntary and other agreement limits remain, with State/local expense and own communication/cooperation alternatives preserved. No blanket deputization or new State removal authority follows from funding. Paragraph (10) funds VOICE staffing/training and nonfinancial assistance to victims of crimes perpetrated by aliens present without authorization. This is the stated conditional purpose, not a finding that any person committed a crime, that status alone proves wrongdoing, or that every victim receives cash. Paragraph (11) funds OPLA attorneys/support staff representing DHS in immigration enforcement and removal proceedings, preserving the Senate scope rather than the House removal-only purpose. Each remains a funding purpose, not an observed workforce, crime, representation, agreement or expenditure. Previously reviewed family-unity paragraph (8) retains its separate conditions. Other package components remain unfinished. Selected Senate CBP operations use their own account and temporal rules. Senate 90002(a)(1) adds $4.1 billion for fiscal year 2025 CBP hiring/training, including field support personnel; (2) adds $2,052,630,000 for eligible recruitment bonuses, performance awards or annual retention bonuses; and (3) adds $855 million for existing patrol-unit repair and additional-unit lease/acquisition, without the House marked-only word. Each of those three paragraphs expressly remains available until September 30, 2029. Paragraph (4) separately adds $5 billion for lease, acquisition, construction, design or improvement of facilities and checkpoints owned, leased or operated by CBP but does not print the same until-September-2029 phrase. Question 45 reserves its precise availability application; that date is not silently extended to (4), nor is a different expiry assumed. Subsection (b) prohibits using subsection (a) funds to recruit, hire or train processing-coordinator personnel after October 31, 2028, not an immediate blanket coordinator ban or a repeal of the funded screening purposes. The House restriction scope/date and ICE bonus service conditions are not substituted. Senate 90004 adds $6.168 billion for fiscal year 2025 CBP purposes, available until September 30, 2029, as one listed-purpose envelope rather than House separate technology earmarks. Its purposes include nonintrusive equipment/related technology for narcotics entry or exit at ports and named borders; Air/Marine platforms; surveillance; referenced biometric entry/exit; screening persons entering or exiting; initial UAC screening consistent with TVPRA; border/drug trafficking efforts; and commemorations. Its tower restriction applies to subsection (a) funds for towers along the southwest and northern borders: the same tower must have both been tested and been accepted by CBP to deliver autonomous capabilities. It does not print the House Federal-Government accepting authority or the same fund/geographic scope. The Senate autonomous definition concerns a system designed for algorithmic real-time detection, identification, classification and tracking and operational adjustments without active/continuous human control. This is a definition/procurement boundary, not proven capability, a new adjudication rule or a guarantee against errors. Complete material biometric-system authority retains its original data-category, accuracy/access/misuse/correction/appeals and other conditions, without a new every-traveller biometric mandate or actual immigration outcome from funding. Initial UAC screening retains the full statutory UAC definition and is expressly consistent with TVPRA. Full material child-screening, transfer and placement protections remain bound; this does not import House age-12 tattoo examinations, sponsor disclosure or disputed withdrawal application, establish an actual finding, or create universal child detention/return. Senate 90007 separately adds DHS $10 billion for fiscal year 2025, available until September 30, 2029, to reimburse costs of activities supporting the named border-safeguarding mission. It does not itself state a State-only beneficiary or the distinct other reimbursement sections' January date; those mechanisms are not merged, and no actual reimbursement or new enforcement power follows. Senate 100053 separately adds DHS/FLETC $750 million for fiscal year 2025, available until September 30, 2029. Not less than $285 million is for training newly hired Federal law enforcement personnel employed by DHS and State and local law enforcement agencies operating in support of DHS. Not more than $465 million is for the listed facility procurement/construction/maintenance/improvement/training-equipment/related expenses. These are a training floor and facilities ceiling within the envelope, not two exact House-sized earmarks; the training categories and facility purposes retain their own Senate scope. All selected funding remains proposed appropriations/purposes, not observed hires, awards, training, data outcomes, costs reimbursed or actual expenditures. Other agency/enforcement and package components remain unfinished. Selected Senate 100054 EOIR, State/local grants and incarceration purposes share the additional $3.33 billion fiscal year 2025 DOJ account, available through September 30, 2029. This is a multi-purpose envelope, not the entire amount earmarked for any selected purpose or the separate House $1.25 billion/$950 million allocations. Paragraph (1) funds immigration judges/support to address the petitions/cases/removals backlog. Effective November 1, 2028, it states EOIR shall comprise not more than 800 immigration judges plus necessary support. That is a proposed ceiling and effective date, not a target minimum, actual workforce, inferred number of cuts or proven backlog change. Paragraph (7) covers the specified State/political-subdivision incarceration compensation and its complete eligibility/limitation. The new incarceration-compensation criteria require a felony conviction or at least two misdemeanor convictions in every listed case. In addition, one of three alternatives must hold. The alien entered without inspection or at a time or place not designated by DHS. Alternatively, the alien was subject to removal proceedings when taken into State/local custody. Alternatively, the alien was admitted as a nonimmigrant and, at that custody time, failed to maintain the admitted or changed nonimmigrant status or comply with its conditions. Those entry/proceeding/status alternatives do not remove the common conviction requirement; a charge, one misdemeanor, any noncitizen status or mere encounter is not substituted. They do not themselves establish a new crime, removal ground or individual custody/status/conviction finding. The compensation limitation excludes the State/local entity if it prohibits or in any way restricts the specified federal/State/local personnel from any of the listed activities: immigration-law compliance; federal-enforcement assistance/cooperation; or the named citizenship/status/admissibility/deportability/custody-information inquiries, federal encounter notifications or responses to federal information requests. The incorporated immigration-laws definition includes its named laws, conventions and treaties; it is not new independent State removal authority. This is the printed funding limitation, not a finding that any State is disqualified, a label for every local policy or a conclusion about constitutional enforceability. Its original exclusion/deportation and Attorney General wording is preserved, distinct from the new removal/DHS wording. Its mixed-election exception requires all three conditions: the election is partly for another purpose; State constitutional/statutory or local-ordinance authority permits alien voting for that other purpose; and that voting is conducted independently so the alien can vote for the other purpose but has no opportunity to vote for the named federal offices. Its separate nonapplication rule also requires all three conditions: each natural parent, or each adoptive parent for an adopted alien, is or was a citizen; permanent U.S. residence before age 16; and reasonable belief in U.S. citizenship at the time of voting. Senate 100051(8) and (11) are purposes within the additional $2,055,000,000 fiscal year 2025 appropriation to the Secretary of Homeland Security, available through September 30, 2029. Paragraph (8) funds removal operations for specified unaccompanied alien children, but amounts under this paragraph shall only be used for permitting a specified unaccompanied alien child to withdraw the application for admission of the child pursuant to section 235(a)(4). The Secretary of Homeland Security must determine on a case-by-case basis all three specified-child conditions. First, the child has been found by an immigration officer at a land border or port of entry of the United States and is inadmissible under the Immigration and Nationality Act. Second, the child has not been a victim of severe forms of trafficking in persons, and there is no credible evidence that such child is at risk of being trafficked upon return of the child to the child's country of nationality or country of last habitual residence. Third, the child does not have a fear of returning to the child's country of nationality or country of last habitual residence owing to a credible fear of persecution. The paragraph does not print the House express contiguous-or-non-contiguous-country phrase or an independent-decision finding; neither is silently inserted into its definition. The Senate 90005(b) State Border Security Reinforcement Fund is a distinct DHS fund. Its complete selected operative clauses are retained below. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 1: There is established, in the Department of Homeland Security, a fund to be known as the ``State Border Security Reinforcement Fund.'' Senate 90005(b) paragraph 2: The Secretary of Homeland Security shall use amounts appropriated or otherwise made available for the Fund for grants to eligible States and units of local government for any of the following purposes: Senate 90005(b) purpose A: Construction or installation of a border wall, border fencing or other barrier, or buoys along the southern border of the United States, which may include planning, procurement of materials, and personnel costs related to such construction or installation. Senate 90005(b) purpose B: Any work necessary to prepare the ground at or near land borders to allow construction and maintenance of a border wall or other barrier fencing. Senate 90005(b) purpose C: Detection and interdiction of illicit substances and aliens who have unlawfully entered the United States and have committed a crime under Federal, State, or local law, and transfer or referral of such aliens to the Department of Homeland Security as provided by law. Senate 90005(b) purpose D: Relocation of aliens who are unlawfully present in the United States from small population centers to other domestic locations. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 3: In addition to amounts otherwise available for the purposes described in paragraph (2), there is appropriated for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, to the Department of Homeland Security for the State Border Security Reinforcement Fund established by paragraph (1), $10,000,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2034, for qualified expenses for such purposes. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 4: The Secretary of Homeland Security may provide grants from the fund established by paragraph (1) to State agencies and units of local governments for expenditures made for completed, ongoing, or new activities, in accordance with law, that occurred on or after January 20, 2021. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 5: Each State desiring to apply for a grant under this subsection shall submit an application to the Secretary containing such information in support of the application as the Secretary may require. The Secretary shall require that each State include in its application the purposes for which the State seeks the funds and a description of how the State plans to allocate the funds. The Secretary shall begin to accept applications not later than 90 days after the date of the enactment of this Act. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 6: Nothing in this subsection shall authorize any State or local government to exercise immigration or border security authorities reserved exclusively to the Federal Government under the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq.) or the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 101 et seq.). The Federal Emergency Management Agency may use not more than 1 percent of the funds made available under this subsection for the purpose of administering grants provided for in this section. Transfer or referral remains as provided by law. Only (A) specifies the southern border; (B) says at or near land borders.
